title: Shortest Way Out of the Maze
statement:
You get a maze as a grid of characters: "." is an open cell and "+" is a wall. You stand on the open cell entrance = [row, col]. Each step moves you one cell up, down, left or right onto an open cell. You cannot leave the grid by walking off it.

An exit is an open cell on the outer border of the grid. The cell you start on never counts as an exit, even if it is on the border.

Return the fewest steps needed to reach any exit, or -1 if no exit can be reached.

examples.why: One step up reaches the border cell (0, 2). The exit at (1, 0) is 2 steps away; the one at (2, 3) is walled off.
You start on the border, but that cell does not count. The only other open cell, (1, 1), is not on the border.
Left twice along row 1, then down column 1 to (4, 1) on the bottom edge.

constraints: entrance is inside the grid and maze[entrance] is "."
hints: Every step costs the same. Which search finds the closest target first when all edges have equal weight?
Breadth-first search from the entrance visits cells in order of distance. The first border cell it reaches is the answer.
Mark the entrance as visited before you start, and test for an exit when you discover a neighbour, not only when you pop it. That way the entrance can never be reported as its own exit.

explain.intuition:
Think of the maze as a graph: open cells are nodes, and neighbouring open cells are joined by an edge of length 1. With equal edge lengths, breadth-first search explores in rings: first every cell 1 step away, then every cell 2 steps away, and so on. So the first exit BFS touches is a nearest one, and you can stop right there.

Depth-first search does not work for this: it finds a way out, not the shortest. The only special rule is that the entrance itself is not an exit, which you handle by checking for exits only on newly discovered neighbours.
steps: Put the entrance in a queue with distance 0 and mark it visited.
Pop a cell. For each of its four neighbours that is inside the grid, open, and not visited: mark it visited.
If that neighbour is on the border, return the current distance + 1.
pitfalls: Counting the entrance as an exit when it sits on the border. In the second example the answer is -1, not 0.
Marking cells visited when popping instead of when pushing. The same cell gets queued many times and big mazes slow down a lot.
Using DFS and returning the first exit found. It is a valid path, not necessarily the shortest.

solutions.title: Relax distances until stable
solutions.idea: Start with distance 0 at the entrance and infinity elsewhere. Sweep the grid, lowering each cell to a neighbour's distance + 1, until a sweep changes nothing. Then take the smallest distance among exits.

solutions.title: Breadth-first search
solutions.idea: BFS explores cells in order of distance, so the first border cell it discovers is a nearest exit.

followups: Return the path itself, not just its length.
Some cells cost 2 steps to cross (mud). What replaces the plain queue?
